extracted.intended_audience: readers of 9to5Mac / general tech-news audience (interested in Apple and related PR matters)
extracted.subtask_description: Reporting on a company's public response to backlash over an advertisement, showing actions taken (apology, cancellation of paid promotion, statements) and messaging choices. Useful as an implicit checklist for crisis/PR responses to ad controversy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Issue a timely public apology
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple issued a public apology to Ad Age saying it “missed the mark with this video.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apologize publicly and promptly through a reputable outlet or direct statement. Use clear language that acknowledges the mistake (example quote: “We missed the mark with this video, and we’re sorry.”). Timing matters — respond soon after backlash emerges to show responsiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge affected stakeholders
rubrics_metrics.description: The piece notes that the concept “didn’t go over well with creators,” and Apple’s statement references creatives and empowering them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly recognize who was upset or harmed (e.g., creators, artists) and speak to their concerns. Naming the impacted group shows awareness and empathy rather than a generic corporate statement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cancel planned paid promotion/TV campaign as corrective action
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple said its plans to run the ad on TV have been cancelled; the ad “had not received any paid media” yet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ad will be amplified via paid channels, halt those plans to prevent further spread while issues are addressed. Note whether paid promotion had already begun; cancelling planned media is a concrete corrective step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use official and public channels to communicate the response
rubrics_metrics.description: The ad and related messages were posted to Tim Cook’s Twitter account and Apple’s YouTube channel, and the apology was issued to Ad Age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliver the apology and updates via owned channels (company/CEO social accounts, official YouTube) and trusted media outlets to ensure the message reaches broad and relevant audiences and is recorded publicly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide and communicate whether to remove or keep the content live
rubrics_metrics.description: As of reporting, the video remained live on both platforms despite the apology and cancelled TV plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose whether removing the content or leaving it accessible better serves transparency and damage control; communicate that decision and rationale. Leaving content live can be framed as transparency, removing it can limit further harm — explain the choice to stakeholders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose origin of the creative (in-house vs agency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad Age says the ad was created in-house by Apple, rather than by an outside agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be transparent about who produced the work when accountability is an issue. Identifying whether creative decisions were in-house or by an external partner informs responsibility and corrective steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frame the apology within the brand’s values and mission
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple’s statement: “Creativity is in our DNA… Our goal is to always celebrate the myriad of ways users express themselves and bring their ideas to life through iPad.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When apologizing, reiterate core brand values and how the organization intends to uphold them. This reassures audiences that the incident is inconsistent with the company’s stated mission and that future work will aim to reflect those values.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use measured, responsibility-taking language rather than deflection
rubrics_metrics.description: Apple’s wording — “We missed the mark with this video, and we’re sorry.” — accepts responsibility without elaborate excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a tone that accepts responsibility succinctly. Avoid defensive or minimizing language; concise acceptance can be more effective than over-explaining or shifting blame.
